patent.title: The turn of the sea
patent.narrative: A short run and an easy one, and the Casa gives it to men it has not made up its mind about. Madeira is five hundred miles south-west and the north-easterly will put you there in a week without your having to think about it. Load sugar. Then come home by way of Terceira, in the Azores, which is eight hundred miles to the north-west of Madeira and in the wrong direction entirely — because the wind that carried you down will not carry you back, and the pilots of the Casa will tell you that the way home from the south is out into the ocean until the wind changes hands, and that a man who has not done it does not believe them. Go and do it. Then you will be trusted with the Guinea run.

log.text: A man who had walked a long way speaks of a town some 15 days' sail to the south, of the Mandinka, with a king in it and a harbour. He was very sure of it, which is not the same as being right.
The São Cristóvão lies in the Tagus, stored and watered. Whatever happens after this is written in this book.
Took the King’s charge: the Guinea run, to Mina and home.
Laid off a course for Funchal.
Bought 60 piece of panos de lã at 3.2 the piece, 195 cruzados in all. Common.
Watered and victualled for 90 days at a cost of 26 cruzados.
Practice has made you better at leadership: 1 point to spend.
Weighed and made sail. Wind 344° NNW, 12 knots.
Laid off a course for Mark.

The pilot: "Mind the tide here, senhor. It makes and takes 3.2 metres twice a day in this water, and every sounding you get is that much of a lie unless you know what the water is doing when you get it. It is half flood now, and high water in 2h24."

Ran the coast in sight all forenoon. It is on the Lisbon chart, but on it the way a thing is when nobody who drew it had been there — a line copied from a line. It is ours now, with a pilot’s name against it.
A gannet came aboard and would not be driven off, heading starboard. There is land that way, and not far.
Noon. 34 miles made good in the 6 hours since she sailed, latitude 38° 28.9' N by the reckoning. 41 miles still to run for Mark.
Noon. 128 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 36° 56.0' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 387 miles still to run for Mark.
Dusk bell. the pilot's doubt has grown to 30 miles. The clock is down to four times.
Noon. 120 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 35° 16.0' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 271 miles still to run for Mark.
Flying fish came aboard in the night by the dozen. The cook has them all.
Noon. 114 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 33° 43.4' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 162 miles still to run for Mark.
Word from Lisbon: Bartolomeu Dias has returned in the São Pantaleão and reported Mpinda. The court has entered it on the padrão real under his name.

Ran the coast in sight all forenoon. It is on the Lisbon chart, but on it the way a thing is when nobody who drew it had been there — a line copied from a line. It is ours now, with a pilot’s name against it.

Raised the land 267° W after 4 days out of sight of it. The hands are up the shrouds without being told. The pilot will not put a figure on it below 49 miles, which is another way of saying he does not know.
You steered straight for Mark. The coast is up, and whether she lies north or south of us from here is a question the reckoning cannot answer to better than 49 miles. Somebody has to choose.
Bearings on the land put her 33 miles from where the board had her. The pilot moves the board, and says something about the set of the water.
Dawn bell. land or a sail has been raised. The clock is down to four times.
Noon. 123 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 22.0' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 40 miles still to run for Mark.
Dusk bell. the pilot's doubt has grown to 16 miles. The clock is down to four times.
Made Mark, and shaped a course for Mark: 2 marks left of the passage.
Noon. 81 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 00.0' N by the reckoning. Ordinary enough. 38 miles still to run for Funchal.
A branch went by with leaves on it, and after it a bundle of reeds.
Dawn bell. the pilot's doubt has grown to 26 miles. The clock is down to four times.
Noon. 29 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 15.4' N by the reckoning. Poor. The hands have noticed. 22 miles still to run for Funchal.
Noon. 34 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 35.5' N by the reckoning. Poor. The hands have noticed. 2 miles still to run for Funchal.
Stood on as she was heading. The pilot said nothing, loudly.
Noon. 136 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 37.3' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 4 miles still to run for Funchal.
Noon. 126 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 35.7' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 4 miles still to run for Funchal.
Stood on as she was heading. The pilot said nothing, loudly.
Dawn bell. the pilot's doubt has grown to 53 miles. The clock is down to four times.
Noon. 147 miles made good in the twenty-four hours, latitude 32° 39.0' N by the reckoning. A fair day’s work. 4 miles still to run for Funchal.
A sail raised from the masthead, 20 miles off. She is the first thing anybody aboard has seen that was not water in 11 days.

Ran the coast in sight all forenoon. It is on the Lisbon chart, but on it the way a thing is when nobody who drew it had been there — a line copied from a line. It is ours now, with a pilot’s name against it.

Raised the land 344° NNW after 7 days of blue water. No chart aboard shows anything here. The escrivão has been sent for. The pilot has her within a dozen miles and is saying so to anyone who will listen.
You steered straight for Funchal. The coast is up, and whether she lies north or south of us from here is a question the reckoning cannot answer to better than 3 miles. Somebody has to choose.
The strange sail is below the horizon and has not been spoken. Whose she was, and what she was doing out here, are two questions this ship will not be answering.
Margin on cargo at today's bids: +801 on 195 paid.
Spoilage: none.
Men lost: none.
Reckoning at landfall: 9 miles out.
Leg report, Lisboa to Funchal: 11 days against 8 on the Casa's reckoning (+3).

At Funchal, the island pilots talk of Ilha do Brasil: it lies in a fog that lifts one day in seven years, west of Ireland, and the Bristol men have gone looking for it more than once. They put it about 53° north, 16° west, give or take 72 leagues. The pilot has pricked it on the chart with a question mark.
Came to an anchor off Funchal. Sugar terraces climbing out of the sea, and the first landfall on every southbound voyage.
Brás de Sousa, the master: “Sugar and wine, sir, and the last good water before the coast. Fill every cask.”
